Tourism is often described as a source of income, but its effect on nature is a topic of real debate.

On the one hand, tourism can help to protect the environment. Entrance fees to national parks and reserves pay for rangers, cleaning and wildlife programmes. Local people also see that a healthy forest or beach is valuable, so they have a reason to preserve it. In some countries, tourism money has saved endangered animals from hunting. For example, many national parks in Africa depend on visitor fees to protect lions and elephants.

On the other hand, large numbers of visitors can seriously damage fragile places. Tourists leave rubbish, walk off the paths and disturb animals. Hotels and airports use a great deal of energy and water, and flights produce a lot of pollution. In popular areas the sea and the coast often become dirty and overcrowded.

In my opinion, tourism can be good for nature only if it is carefully controlled. For example, governments should limit the number of visitors, ban plastic and teach tourists to respect the places they visit. If this happens, both people and the environment can benefit.
Recent Real 10.10.2026 · 1-smena · Task.C1:
The relationship between tourism and the natural environment is far more nuanced than either camp tends to admit.

Supporters argue, with some justification, that tourism gives nature a price tag. Revenue from park fees and eco-lodges frequently funds conservation work that governments would never afford, and communities that profit from wildlife have little incentive to poach it. Costa Rica's protected forests are often cited as proof that preservation and profit can coexist.

Critics, however, point to the unmistakable damage caused by mass travel. Coral reefs are trampled, trails are eroded and local wildlife is displaced by construction and noise. In addition, local water supplies are often diverted to resorts, leaving nearby villages short. Moreover, the carbon footprint of long-haul flights quietly undermines whatever good a single reserve achieves.

In my view, the outcome depends not on tourism itself but on how it is managed. Strict visitor quotas, high environmental standards for hotels and a genuine share of profits for local residents can turn a threat into an ally. Without such regulation, however, the very landscapes that attract visitors risk being destroyed by them.

Tourism has become one of the biggest industries in the world, and people disagree about what it does to local communities.

Those who support tourism say that it creates jobs and brings money into poor areas. Local people can work in hotels, restaurants and shops, or sell traditional crafts and food. The income can also pay for new roads, schools and hospitals that everyone can use.

However, there are real disadvantages. When many tourists arrive, prices of housing and food often go up, so residents cannot afford to live in their own neighbourhoods. The streets become crowded and noisy, and traditions can lose their meaning when they are performed only for visitors. Sometimes the biggest profits go to foreign companies, not to local families. For example, a small guesthouse owner can hire neighbours and buy food from local farmers.

I believe that tourism is useful when the community has a say in how it develops. For instance, small family guesthouses and local guides keep money in the area, and rules can protect quiet residential zones. With sensible planning, tourism can improve life for local people instead of damaging the places where they live.
Recent Real 10.10.2026 · 1-smena · Task.C1:
Few industries divide opinion in host communities as sharply as tourism, and both sides have a valid case.

Proponents emphasise the economic lifeline it provides. In regions with few alternatives, visitors sustain entire networks of guides, drivers, artisans and restaurateurs, and the tax revenue they generate can finance infrastructure that residents would otherwise lack. Samarkand and Bukhara, for example, have restored historic districts largely thanks to visitor income.

Detractors counter that the benefits are rarely distributed fairly. Rents soar as homes are converted into short-term lets, long-standing residents are priced out, and everyday life is reshaped around the needs of strangers. Cultural practices may also be reduced to staged performances, losing their authenticity. Tour operators based abroad often capture the largest share of the profits, leaving residents with low-paid seasonal work.

On balance, I would argue that tourism is neither a blessing nor a curse in itself. A balanced policy would therefore measure success by residents' wellbeing, not only by visitor numbers. Its impact is determined by governance: caps on holiday rentals, incentives for locally owned businesses and genuine consultation with residents can ensure that growth enriches, rather than erodes, the communities that make a destination worth visiting.

Technology has changed the way we study, and many people ask whether online lessons are better than classes in a school building.

Supporters of online education say that it is more flexible. Students can learn at any time and from any place, so they save money and time on travelling. They can also repeat recorded lessons as many times as they need and choose from courses taught by excellent teachers around the world. For instance, a student in a village can follow an English course from a famous university.

On the other hand, face-to-face education has important strengths. Teachers can see immediately when a student is confused and can explain again in a different way. Students talk to each other, work in groups and learn communication skills that are difficult to practise on a screen. It is also easier to stay focused in a classroom without phones and other distractions.

In my opinion, the best results come from a mixture of both. Online tools are very useful for homework and extra practice, while real lessons give motivation and personal support. Therefore, schools should combine the two methods instead of choosing only one of them.
Recent Real 10.10.2026 · 2-smena · Task.C1:
The debate over whether online education outperforms the traditional classroom is a defining one for modern schooling, and the honest answer is that each excels in different respects.

Advocates of online learning highlight its accessibility and adaptability. Learners in remote regions can reach world-class instruction, and self-paced platforms let them revisit difficult material until it is mastered. For motivated adults juggling work and study, this flexibility is invaluable. Cost matters too: online courses are frequently cheaper, widening access to people who could never afford to relocate.

Nevertheless, face-to-face teaching offers something screens struggle to replicate. Immediate feedback, spontaneous discussion and the structure of a shared timetable sustain motivation, especially among younger students who lack self-discipline. Online learners, by contrast, must supply that self-control themselves. Classrooms also nurture collaboration and social confidence, which are as vital as academic knowledge.

In my view, effectiveness depends less on the medium than on the learner and the quality of teaching. Consequently, a blended model, in which digital resources reinforce in-person guidance, seems the most sensible compromise, combining convenience with the human connection that genuine learning so often requires.

Whether studying online can truly match the classroom experience is a question that has become unavoidable in recent years.

Those who answer in the affirmative note that digital platforms can deliver content just as effectively as a lecture hall. Recorded lessons, interactive exercises and instant assessments allow learners to progress at their own pace, and the absence of a commute frees up valuable study time. Technology has also made online assessment more reliable than it once was, narrowing the gap in results.

Sceptics, however, maintain that a physical school provides advantages no software can fully reproduce. Constant supervision, face-to-face interaction and the routine of attending lessons help students stay engaged, while extracurricular activities develop teamwork and resilience. Results alone, in any case, do not capture the personal development that school life encourages. Furthermore, many learners find it surprisingly difficult to resist distractions at home.

On balance, I believe that the answer varies with the student. Mature, self-disciplined learners may thrive online, whereas younger pupils generally benefit from the guidance and community of a school. Ideally, education systems should offer flexible, blended options so that every learner can choose the format that suits them best.
